source.title: Qwen-Scope: Turning Sparse Features into Development Tools for Large Language Models
source.authors: Bo-Yi Deng; Xu Wang; Yao-Ning Wang; Yunyang Wan; Yubo Ma; Bao-Song Yang; Hao-Ran Wei; Jia-Long Tang; Huan Lin; Rui-Ze Gao; Tian-Hao Li; Qian Cao; Xuan-Cheng Ren; Xiaodong Deng; Anke Yang; Fei Huang; Dayiheng Liu; Jing-Ren Zhou

record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE feature discovery and interventions to Qwen LLMs and reports results bearing on whether SAE dictionaries recover usable sparse features in LLMs; it does not reproduce the toy-network method.
record.gate_note: Tests V4 through SAE-derived features identified in Qwen models and used for classification or interventions. It does not measure feature-direction geometry, neuron overlap, capacity competition, or whether SAE features are complete or canonical. Other application results are omitted when they do not measure whether an SAE dictionary recovers usable features.
record.test_reason: This is an SAE release and applications report. It uses SAE features as tools for steering, toxicity classification, benchmark analysis, data synthesis, SFT and RL, and reports how well those methods work. It gives no reconstruction fidelity, interpretability rates or other test of whether the dictionaries recover sparse features. It also never measures feature geometry, neuron overlap, capacity, completeness or dimensionality. The rows report application performance (classifier F1, steering outcomes), not whether a version of superposition holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude SAEs can serve as reusable interfaces for diagnosing, steering, evaluating and improving LLMs. They make no claim about superposition geometry or canonical units.
record.recipe_differences: The report trains and applies sparse autoencoders to Qwen LLM activations and demonstrates downstream uses; it does not reproduce the original toy-network experiments or their geometric measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with model size, layer, language, and steering or ablation strength. Cross-lingual transfer is uneven, and larger-model transfer is described as stronger and more stable.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen3-1.7B and 8B, a few SAE features used as an OR-rule classifier reach best-layer English toxicity F1 above 0.90. Transfer from English to other languages is uneven.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features in LLMs are usable as sparse concept detectors for downstream classification.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating or adding single SAE feature directions changes code-switching, style and repetition. Ablating an irrelevant language feature has negligible effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single SAE feature directions act as causal steering handles for specific behaviours.

record.problems: No direct test of feature geometry, neuron-level distribution, or completeness against a known ground truth. Many steering examples are qualitative case studies; several figure values are not stated in the text. Cross-lingual transfer values are not reliably recoverable from the flattened figure text.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted application results on benchmark redundancy, safety-data synthesis, SFT, and RL where the reported outcome concerns downstream workflow performance rather than whether an SAE dictionary recovers usable sparse features. Also omitted quantitative cross-lingual per-language values in Figure 9 because the extracted figure text does not reliably map values to languages.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep or geometry.
No test of capacity competition or of dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of other causes of polysemanticity.
No measurement of features spread across neurons. No reconstruction or interpretability evaluation of the SAE dictionaries; the SAEs are only used as tools.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicality. The repetition feature firing in both benign and pathological repetition is anecdotal and not framed as such a test.
No test of 1-D versus multidimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T3' with V4 'supports' overreads an applications report. The paper gives no evidence on whether SAE dictionaries faithfully recover the model's sparse features. It reports no reconstruction loss, no interpretability scoring, and only a passing mention of negligible dead features. All results are the performance of the SAE-based methods. The reader's text also says the five models in Section 7 are Qwen-only; they are Gemma-2, Llama-3.1 and Qwen3.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-over-dimension sweep, sparsity transition, or regular geometry are tested.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons result from capacity pressure or whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity indicates superposition.

Tests SAE feature discovery and use in selected Qwen models, but not whether features are distributed across many neurons or whether the dictionaries recover a complete account of model representations.
Does not test completeness, stability, or canonicality of SAE features.
Uses SAE feature directions but does not test whether model features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Qwen3-1.7B
rows.operation_detail: Selected top toxic-biased SAE features and applied an OR-rule classifier to held-out English text.

conditions.value: top K toxic-biased SAE features; K ∈ {1, 2, 5, 10}; best layer selected by held-out performance

rows.note: The authors report that an SAE feature set classifies toxicity without training an additional classifier; exact best F1 is not stated.
rows.check: This is the F1 of the study's own rule-based classifier, a method-performance result rather than a test of V4. The best layer was picked on held-out performance, so it is a selection value and optimistic. No baseline classifier is compared.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Selected top toxic-biased SAE features and applied an OR-rule classifier to held-out English text.

conditions.value: top K toxic-biased SAE features; K ∈ {1, 2, 5, 10}; best layer selected by held-out performance

rows.note: The authors report that an SAE feature set classifies toxicity without training an additional classifier; exact best F1 is not stated.
rows.check: Same as R1: method performance with the best layer picked on held-out data, and no baseline comparison.

rows.subject: Qwen3 models
rows.operation_detail: Suppressed the highly activated Chinese-language SAE feature during generation.
rows.measure: Whether feature suppression removes unexpected language mixing
rows.baseline: The response unexpectedly mixed Chinese text into English.
rows.value: The unexpected language mixing was removed while the intended English response was preserved.
rows.note: The paper does not identify the specific Qwen3 checkpoint for this case study.
rows.check: A single qualitative steering case study and an application demonstration. The checkpoint is unspecified and no rate is reported.

rows.subject: Qwen3 models
rows.operation_detail: Activated an SAE feature associated with classical Chinese during generation.
rows.measure: Whether feature activation changes generated style
rows.value: The continuation shifted toward classical literary style while preserving the semantic direction of the prompt.
rows.note: The paper does not identify the specific Qwen3 checkpoint for this case study.
rows.check: A single qualitative style-transfer example. No rate is reported and the checkpoint is unspecified.

rows.subject: Five models (not individually named in this result)
rows.operation_detail: Directional ablation of the identified target-language feature at the final layer immediately before the first unexpected switch token.

conditions.value: different ablation coefficients; exact values not stated

rows.baseline: Unablated code-switching ratio; numeric value not stated
rows.value: Ablation consistently reduced the code-switching ratio; larger coefficients produced greater reductions.
rows.note: The text reports a consistent effect across all five models but does not name them in this result passage; plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Section 7.4 names the five models as spanning Gemma-2, Llama-3.1 and Qwen3, not Qwen-only. This is an ablation effect on code-switching, not a test of superposition. Values are plotted only and not transcribed.

rows.subject: Five models (not individually named in this result)
rows.operation_detail: Ablated an irrelevant language feature as a control for target-feature ablation.
rows.baseline: Unablated code-switching ratio; numeric value not stated
rows.note: The text does not name the five models in this result passage.
rows.check: Control for R5; same subject correction applies (Gemma-2, Llama-3.1 and Qwen3). It does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Suppressed an identified repetition-related SAE feature on repetition-prone samples.
rows.baseline: Baseline repetition ratio; exact value not stated
rows.value: Suppressing the feature consistently reduced repetition below baseline.
rows.note: The paper states that bidirectional steering verified a causal link between the identified SAE feature and repetitive behavior; plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: A steering effect on repetition, with values only in Figure 20. This is an application result, not a measure of superposition.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Amplified an identified repetition-related SAE feature on normal samples.
rows.measure: Whether the output exhibits repetitive behavior
rows.baseline: Normal samples without feature amplification; numeric rate not stated
rows.value: Amplifying the feature successfully induced repetitive behavior.
rows.note: The paper reports a behavioral effect but does not provide a numeric rate in the text.
rows.check: A steering-induced behaviour with no numeric rate given. This is an application result.

rows.subject: Qwen3-1.7B
rows.operation_detail: Applied English-discovered SAE features to held-out examples in other languages without rediscovering features.

conditions.value: English and other languages; language-specific values are not reliably available in the extracted figure text

rows.baseline: Features rediscovered separately for each language; numeric comparison not stated
rows.value: Transfer was strong for English and several European languages, including Russian and French, and substantially harder for distant languages such as Arabic, Chinese, and especially Amharic.
rows.uncertainty: IQR shown in Figure 9 for layer-wise mean transfer F1; numerical bounds not stated
rows.note: Qualitative summary only; the individual plotted language values cannot be assigned reliably from the flattened figure text.
rows.check: Cross-lingual transfer of the study's own classifier, a method-performance result. Figure 9d gives per-language best F1 roughly between 0.53 and 0.92, but these are best-layer selection values.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Applied English-discovered SAE features to held-out examples in other languages without rediscovering features.

conditions.value: English and other languages; language-specific values are not reliably available in the extracted figure text

rows.baseline: Features rediscovered separately for each language; numeric comparison not stated
rows.value: Transfer was strong for English and several European languages, including Russian and French, and substantially harder for distant languages such as Arabic, Chinese, and especially Amharic; the larger model improved the level and stability of transfer overall.
rows.uncertainty: IQR shown in Figure 9 for layer-wise mean transfer F1; numerical bounds not stated
rows.note: Qualitative summary only; the individual plotted language values cannot be assigned reliably from the flattened figure text.
rows.check: Same as R9: method performance on best-layer selection values.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Selected Qwen3 models; English toxicity classification and the reported SAE steering examples
reader_labels.reason: SAE-derived features were identified and used to classify or causally alter model outputs (R1–R5, R7–R8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: English-discovered toxicity features transferred across languages in Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B
reader_labels.reason: Transfer was uneven: several languages were supported, while distant languages were substantially harder (R9–R10).
